blocks.markdown: The Supreme Court commonly states **three elements** of the first paragraph of Section 1 of B.P. Blg. 22: **(1) issuance of a check to apply on account or for value; (2) knowledge at issuance of insufficient funds or credit; and (3) subsequent dishonor** for the statutory reason, including an unjustified stop-payment order where applicable. The prosecution must prove **every element beyond reasonable doubt**.

table.caption: Verbatim — B.P. Blg. 22, Section 1 (Checks without sufficient funds)
rows:
SEC. 1. Checks without sufficient funds.—Any person who makes or draws and issues any check to apply on account or for value, knowing at the time of issue that he does not have sufficient funds in or credit with the drawee bank for the payment of such check in full upon its presentment, which check is subsequently dishonored by the drawee bank for insufficiency of funds or credit or would have been dishonored for the same reason had not the drawer, without any valid reason, ordered the bank to stop payment, shall be punished by imprisonment of not less than thirty days but not more than one (1) year or by a fine of not less than but not more than double the amount of the check which fine shall in no case exceed Two Hundred Thousand Pesos, or both such fine and imprisonment at the discretion of the court.

The same penalty shall be imposed upon any person who, having sufficient funds in or credit with the drawee bank when he makes or draws and issues a check, shall fail to keep sufficient funds or to maintain a credit to cover the full amount of the check if presented within a period of ninety (90) days from the date appearing thereon, for which reason it is dishonored by the drawee bank.

Where the check is drawn by a corporation, company or entity, the person or persons who actually signed the check in behalf of such drawer shall be liable under this Act.

blocks.markdown: The check must be issued **to apply on account or for value** — in practical terms, connected to an account or value in the way the law requires. The prosecutor must still prove the other elements, especially the issuer's knowledge of insufficient funds and the check's dishonor. For a **corporate check**, the person or persons who actually signed on behalf of the corporation may be liable under this section.

rows: Read this carefully  Idos is not a broad rule that every “guarantee check” is exempt. Its holding turns on the evidence: the check merely evidenced a partner’s future share and was not issued for a present account or value. Compare it with Que v. People below.

blocks.markdown: Check as mere guarantee: Que v. People

sourceRefs.section: 2(a)(i). Check as mere guarantee — Que v. People

blocks.markdown: Simple explanation: a drawer generally **cannot escape B.P. Blg. 22 simply by saying the check was intended only as a deposit or guarantee**. The Supreme Court has held that the law does not create an exception for checks issued as guarantees. But the prosecution still needs to prove **all statutory elements**; Idos illustrates that a separate failure to prove “on account or for value” can matter.
